{{technical|date=April 2022}}

In [[Umbral calculus]], the '''Bernoulli umbra''' <math>B_-</math> is an [[umbra (mathematics)|umbra]], a formal symbol, defined by the relation <math>\operatorname{eval}B_-^n=B^-_n</math>, where <math>\operatorname{eval}</math> is the index-lowering operator,<ref>{{Cite book|citeseerx = 10.1.1.11.7516|chapter = Difference Equations via the Classical Umbral Calculus|year = 1998|pages = 397–411|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-4108-9_21|isbn=978-1-4612-8656-1|title= Mathematical Essays in honor of Gian-Carlo Rota|last1= Taylor|first1= Brian D.}}</ref> also known as evaluation operator <ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Di Nardo |first1=E. |title=A new approach to Sheppard's corrections |date=February 14, 2022 |class=math.ST |eprint= 1004.4989 }}</ref> and <math>B^-_n</math> are [[Bernoulli numbers]], called ''moments'' of the umbra.<ref>{{cite journal |title=The classical umbral calculus: Sheffer sequences |journal= Lecture Notes of Seminario Interdisciplinare di Matematica |date= 2009  |volume= 8  |pages = 101–130 |url=http://math.fau.edu/Niederhausen/HTML/Papers/The%20classical%20umbral%20calculus%20dinardo_09.pdf}}</ref> A similar umbra, defined as <math>\operatorname{eval}B_+^n=B^+_n</math>, where <math>B^+_1=1/2</math> is also often used and sometimes called Bernoulli umbra as well. They are related by equality <math>B_+=B_-+1</math>. Along with the [[Euler umbra]], Bernoulli umbra is one of the most important umbras.

In [[Levi-Civita field]], Bernoulli umbras can be represented by elements with [[power series]] <math>B_-= \varepsilon^{-1} -\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\varepsilon }{24}+\frac{3 \varepsilon ^3}{640}-\frac{1525 \varepsilon ^5}{580608}+\dotsb</math> and <math>B_+= \varepsilon^{-1} +\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\varepsilon }{24}+\frac{3 \varepsilon ^3}{640}-\frac{1525 \varepsilon ^5}{580608}+\dotsb</math>, with lowering index operator corresponding to taking the coefficient of <math>1=\varepsilon^0</math> of the power series. The numerators of the terms are given in OEIS A118050<ref>{{Cite OEIS|1=A118050|mode=cs2}}</ref> and the denominators are in OEIS A118051.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|1=A118051|mode=cs2}}</ref> Since the coefficients of <math>\varepsilon^{-1}</math> are non-zero, the both are infinitely large numbers, <math>B_-</math> being infinitely close (but not equal, a bit smaller) to <math>\varepsilon^{-1}-1/2</math> and <math>B_+</math> being infinitely close (a bit smaller) to <math>\varepsilon^{-1}+1/2</math>.

In [[Hardy field]]s (which are generalizations of Levi-Civita field) umbra <math>B_+</math> corresponds to the [[germ (mathematics)|germ]] at infinity of the function <math>\psi^{-1}(\ln x)</math> while <math>B_-</math> corresponds to the germ at infinity of <math>\psi^{-1}(\ln x)-1</math>, where <math>\psi^{-1}(x)</math> is inverse [[digamma function]].
[[File:Bumbra.png|thumb|Plot of the function <math>\psi^{-1}(\ln(x))</math>, whose germ at positive infinity corresponds to <math>B_+</math>.]]

==Exponentiation==

Since [[Bernoulli polynomials]] is a generalization of Bernoulli numbers, exponentiation of Bernoulli umbra can be expressed via [[Bernoulli polynomials]]:

:<math>\operatorname{eval} (B_-+a)^n=B_n(a),</math>

where <math>a</math> is a real or [[complex number]].
This can be further generalized using [[Hurwitz Zeta function]]:

:<math>\operatorname{eval} (B_-+a)^p=-p\zeta(1-p,a).</math>

From the [[Riemann_zeta_function#Riemann's_functional_equation|Riemann functional equation]] for Zeta function it follows that

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\,B_+^{-p}=\operatorname{eval}\frac{B_+^{p+1} 2^p\pi^{p+1}}{\sin(\pi p/2)\Gamma(p)(p+1)}</math>

==Derivative rule==

Since <math>B^+_1=1/2</math> and <math>B^-_1=-1/2</math> are the only two members of the sequences <math>B^+_n</math> and <math>B^-_n</math> that differ, the following rule follows for any analytic function <math>f(x)</math>:

:<math>f'(x)=\operatorname{eval}(f(B_++x)-f(B_-+x))=\operatorname{eval} \Delta f(B_-+x)</math>

==Elementary functions of Bernoulli umbra==

As a general rule, the following formula holds for any analytic function <math>f(x)</math>:

:<math>\operatorname{eval}f(B_-+x)=\frac{D}{e^D-1} f(x).</math>

This allows to derive expressions for elementary functions of Bernoulli umbra.

:<math>\operatorname{eval} \cos (z B_-)=\operatorname{eval} \cos (z B_+)=\frac z2 \cot \left(\frac z2\right)</math>

:<math>\operatorname{eval} \cosh (z B_-)=\operatorname{eval} \cosh (z B_+)=\frac z2 \coth \left(\frac z2\right)</math>

:<math>\operatorname{eval} e^{z B_-}=\frac{z}{e^{z}-1}</math>

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\ln ( B_-+z)=\psi(z)</math>

Particularly,

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\ln  B_+=-\gamma</math> <ref>{{Cite arXiv |eprint = 1011.3352|last1 = Yu|first1 = Yiping|title = Bernoulli Operator and Riemann's Zeta Function|year = 2010|class = math.NT}}</ref>

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\frac1{\pi }\ln \left(\frac{ B _+-\frac{z}{\pi }}{ B _-+\frac{z}{\pi }}\right)=\cot z</math>

:<math>\operatorname{eval} \frac1\pi\ln \left(\frac{B _-+1/2 +\frac{z}{\pi }}{B _-+1/2 -\frac{z}{\pi }}\right)=\tan z</math>

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\cos (a B_-+x) = \frac{a}{2} \csc \left(\frac{a}{2}\right) \cos \left(\frac{a}{2}-  x\right)</math>

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\sin (a B_-+x) = \frac{a}{2} \cot \left(\frac{a}{2}\right) \sin x -\frac{a}{2} \cos x </math>

Particularly,

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\sin  B_-=-1/2</math>, 
:<math>\operatorname{eval}\sin  B_+=1/2</math>,

==Relations between exponential and logarithmic functions==

Bernoulli umbra allows to establish relations between exponential, trigonometric and hyperbolic functions on one side and logarithms, inverse trigonometric and inverse hyperbolic functions on the other side in closed form:

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\left(\cosh \left(2 x  B _\pm\right)-1\right)=\operatorname{eval}\frac{x}{\pi} \operatorname{artanh}\left(\frac{x}{\pi B _\pm}\right)=\operatorname{eval}\frac{x}{\pi} \operatorname{arcoth}\left(\frac{\pi   B _\pm}{x}\right)=x \coth (x)-1</math>

:<math>\operatorname{eval}\frac{z}{2\pi }\ln \left(\frac{ B _+-\frac{z}{2\pi }}{ B _-+\frac{z}{2\pi }}\right)=\operatorname{eval} \cos (z B_-)=\operatorname{eval} \cos (z B_+)=\frac z2 \cot \left(\frac z2\right)</math>
